title: SYSK Selects: How Guide Dogs Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun chosen by Josh, "How Guide Dogs Work." The hosts trace guide dog history from early German training in Potsdam for blinded WWI veterans, through Dorothy Harris Eustace and Morris Frank founding The Seeing Eye in Tennessee. They describe guide dog work: stopping at every curb, selective disobedience at intersections, obstacle awareness, staying out of the way in public, and not being petted while working. They cover the process of puppy raising (about 6 weeks to 18 months), intensive school training, weeding out dogs (roughly 400 puppies to about 140 graduates), handler matching and month-long training, praise-based rather than treat-based training, retirement at 8 to 10 years, and becoming an instructor. Episode ends with a potty-training tangent and listener mail from Jane Genab, MD, who knits to raise money for Angels Among Us Pet Rescue in Alpharetta, Georgia.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects episode on guide dogs and the hosts open with banter about sound quality and Chuck's health.

segments.title: History of guide dogs and The Seeing Eye
segments.summary: Seeing eye dogs are a brand name from The Seeing Eye, the first American guide dog school. Guide dog training began in Potsdam, Germany, for blinded WWI veterans. Dorothy Harris Eustace wrote about it, and Morris Frank got a dog and founded the Seeing Eye in Tennessee with $10,000.

segments.title: Etiquette around working guide dogs
segments.summary: Hosts explain that working guide dogs should be left alone, and that you can ask the handler before petting. Guide dogs are allowed anywhere the public is allowed, and they must concentrate on routes and pacing.

segments.title: Crosswalks, curbs and selective disobedience
segments.summary: Guide dogs are trained to stop at every curb and to master intersections. The dog waits for hazards to clear even when the handler says to go, a behavior called selective disobedience. Hosts also mention pedestrian crossing signals.

segments.title: Guide dog skills and working as a team
segments.summary: Guide dogs learn to find elevator buttons, stop at stairs, lie quietly, and think in human-sized terms such as headroom. The handler chooses the destination and the dog handles obstacles. When the harness is off the dog is a family pet.

segments.title: Housebreaking tangent and dog jobs
segments.summary: The hosts take a tangent into a housebreaking tip for puppies, praising a dog for going on cue. They discuss why guide dogs must toilet on command and talk about Chuck's dogs and whether working dogs are happier.

segments.title: Guide dog schools and costs
segments.summary: Guide dog schools are nonprofits that provide dogs free of charge to recipients. They handle breeding, puppy raising, evaluation, training, instructor training, handler matching, and retirement. Labs, goldens, and German shepherds are common breeds.

segments.title: Puppy raising program
segments.summary: Puppies are evaluated from about six weeks old, and many are weeded out. Volunteer puppy raisers raise them for 12 to 18 months, teaching basic obedience and socialization through praise rather than treats, with about five new experiences a week. Raisers say goodbye when the dog returns to school.

segments.title: Intensive school training and handler matching
segments.summary: Dogs get about six months of intensive training at school, with fake intersections and simulated obstacles. Of roughly 400 puppies, about 140 graduate. Handlers then train for about a month with their matched dog, often in on-site dorms.

segments.title: Becoming an instructor and retirement
segments.summary: Becoming a guide dog instructor requires two to three years as a supervised apprentice and often a college degree; the job is demanding and waitlisted. Dogs retire around eight to ten years old, and may go to the handler, the puppy raiser, or an adopter.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jane Genab and Angels Among Us
segments.summary: Listener Jane Genab, an ER doctor, knits items and donates proceeds to Angels Among Us Pet Rescue in Alpharetta, Georgia, after the loss of her dog Rica. The hosts encourage listeners to support her fundraising goal of six thousand dollars.
